This appeal, preferred under section 10(1)(a) of the 
Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1958 is directed against the 

<<PAGE 2>>
 
2
judgment and order dated 29.08.2019 passed by the learned 
Special Judge, Rangpur in Special Case No. 03 of 2013 arising 
out of Mithapukur Police Station Case No. 33 dated 
18.04.2008, corresponding to G.R. No. 150 of 2008 convicting 
the accused-appellant under Sections 409/109 of the Penal 
Code, read with Section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption 
Act, 1947 and sentencing him to suffer rigorous imprisonment 
for 05(five) years with a fine of Taka 10,000/-(ten thousand), 
in default to suffer rigorous imprisonment for 03(three) months 
more. The convict-appellant was also directed to deposit a sum 
of Taka 2,76,450/- into the Government treasury within 30 
days. 
The facts relevant for disposal of the appeal, in short, are 
that one Md. Hasan Ferdous Sarker,  Upazila Senior Fishery 
Officer, Mithapukur, Rangpur lodged the First Information 
Report (FIR) with Mithapukur Police Station on 18.04.2008 
alleging inter alia that the accused persons were selling the ‘®le¤ 
®f¡e¡’ (fish carp/spawn) in the Mithapukur area at prices 
substantially higher than the Government-fixed rate. The 
Government-fixed rate was Taka 1,300/- per unit, but they 

<<PAGE 3>>
 
3
were selling the same at Taka 2,500/- to 2,800/- per unit. Upon 
receipt of such information, a team of the Rapid Action 
Battalion (RAB) apprehended the accused persons at the scene. 
It was further alleged that they were selling the “®le¤ 
®f¡e¡”(carp/spawn) by using forged money receipts. They had 
been committing the offence for a long time. Thus they had 
misappropriated Government revenue amounting to Taka 
2,76,450/- and thereby committed offence under Sections 
406/420/409/467/471/109 of the Penal Code read with Section 
5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. 
Upon closure of the investigation, the investigating 
officer submitted report bearing charge sheet No. 442 dated 
29.11.2012 against the accused-persons under Section 409 of 
the Penal Code, read with Section 5(2) of the Prevention of 
Corruption Act, 1947. 
Subsequently, the case was transmitted to the learned 
Special Judge, Rangpur and the same was registered as Special 
Case No. 03 of 2013. The charge was framed against the 
accused persons under Section 409 of the Penal Code read with 
Section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 on 

<<PAGE 4>>
 
4
12.05.2013 and the accused-persons pleaded not guilty and 
claimed to be tried when the charge was read out and explained 
to them. 
In the course of the trial, as many as 14 prosecution 
witnesses were examined to prove the indictment while the 
defence adduced none. The accused-persons were examined 
under Section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and they 
reiterated their innocence. 
Upon conclusion of the trial and hearing the parties, the 
learned Special Judge, Rangpur convicted the accused-persons 
under Section 409 and 109 of the Penal Code read with Section 
5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act and sentenced them to 
suffer rigorous imprisonment for 05(five) years with a fine of 
Taka 10,000/-(ten thousand) in default, to suffer rigorous 
imprisonment for 03(three) months more by judgment and 
order dated 29.08.2019. 
Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the said 
judgment and order of conviction and sentence, the convict 
preferred the instant Criminal Appeal before this Court. This 

<<PAGE 5>>
 
5
Court enlarged the appellant on bail for a period of 06(six) 
months on 26.11.2019.  
Mr. Md. Atiqul Haque (Salim) along with Most. Sharifa 
Sultana, the learned Advocates appearing on behalf of the 
appellant contend that the purchasers of the carp being PW7, 
PW9 and PW11 categorically testified that they had purchased 
the fish carp/spawn at the Government-fixed rate. Specifically, 
PW7 in his cross-examination stated that he did not pay any 
amount exceeding the fixed rate. 
He further contends that PW2, who is an owner of a 
press, deposed in his examination-in-chief that the seized 
money receipts had not been printed at his press, and those are 
computer composed, printed by a digital printing process. He 
gave evidence which was adverse to the prosecution case 
concerning the alleged forged receipts, however, he was not 
declared hostile by the prosecution, thereby rendering his 
testimony admissible and undermining the prosecution’s case 
regarding the forged receipts. 
He further contends that the co-accused, Md. Rezaul 
Bari, who was alleged to be the principal offender, and 

<<PAGE 6>>
 
6
manager of the Hatchery preferred Criminal Appeal No. 10477 
of 2019 before this Court, which was allowed and he was 
acquitted by a judgment dated 17.10.2023. Challenging the 
judgment and order of acquittal, the Anti-Corruption 
Commission preferred Criminal Petition for Leave to Appeal 
No. 1605 of 2024 before the Honourable Appellate Division. 
Upon hearing the parties, the Apex Court dismissed the 
Criminal Petition for Leave to Appeal on 11.12.2024. As the 
appellant stands on the same footing and as such he is entitled 
to the same benefit of the said acquittal.  
He submits that the prosecution hopelessly failed to 
prove the case beyond reasonable doubt and the convict-
appellant is entitled to be acquitted of the charge leveled 
against him. 
He finally prays for allowing the appeal. 
Per contra, Mr. Kazi Mohammad Joynal Abedin, learned 
Advocate appearing on behalf of respondent No. 2, submits 
that the prosecution examined as many as 14 witnesses and 
established the prosecution case by adducing both oral and 
documentary evidence.  

<<PAGE 7>>
 
7
He further contends that there is no illegality, 
impropriety or infirmity in the impugned judgment and order 
of conviction and sentence. 
He finally submits that the trial Court very rightly and 
legally passed the impugned judgment and order of conviction 
and sentence, the appeal is devoid of merit and as such the 
appeal is liable to be dismissed.  
I have considered the submissions of the learned 
Advocates for both sides, perused the evidence on record, the 
impugned judgment and order passed by the trial Court and the 
materials on record. 
For a proper adjudication of the matter and analysis of 
the facts on record of the prosecution’s evidence are being

PW1, Md. Hasan Ferdous Sarkar, informant Upazila

In cross-examination, he admitted that the Shathibari

PW2, Md. Maminur Rashid, businessman, and owner of

been printed at his press. The money receipts were printed in

PW3, Md. Abdur Rauf, District Fishery Officer, deposed

In cross-examination, he deposed that he did not know as

The above-mentioned three material witnesses (PW7, 
PW9 and PW11) who were purchasers of carp/spawn 
consistently and categorically stated that they purchased the 
carp at the Government-fixed rate. Their testimony directly 
contradicts the foundational allegation of alleged overpricing 
and is fatal to the prosecution’s case. Their subsequent 
detention by the RAB and the obtaining of their signatures on

16

investigative process. 
The circumstances, in which their signatures were 
obtained, coupled with their categorical denial of having paid 
any excess amount, materially affect the evidentiary value of 
any document purportedly prepared or exhibited based on their 
signatures. Their evidence therefore cannot be brushed aside

To convict a person, there should be unimpeachable 
evidence of a reliable witness beyond any reasonable doubt. If 
any doubt arises in a criminal case, then the benefit of doubt 
should be given to the accused. Suspicion, however strong, 
cannot substitute proof. 
It is an admitted fact that co-accused Rejaul Bari was the 
Manager of the Hatchery and the alleged principal offender 
and the appellant was clerk-cum-typist. The principal accused 
was acquitted by this Court in Criminal Appeal No. 10477 of 
2019 on 17.10.2023. Being aggrieved, the Anti-Corruption 
Commission preferred Criminal Petition for Leave to Appeal 
No. 1605 of 2024 before the Honourable Appellate Division. 
Upon hearing, the Appellate Division dismissed the Criminal 
Petition for Leave to Appeal on 11.12.2024. The appellant, 
being a subordinate employee (clerk-cum-typist) stands on an 
even better footing than the principal accused who has already 

<<PAGE 18>>
 
18
been acquitted. This precedent further strengthens the case for 
the appellant’s acquittal. The principle of parity becomes 
relevant, provided that no distinct and incriminating evidence 
is available against the present appellant. 
It is also significant that the appellant was a clerk-cum-
typist. In the absence of reliable evidence establishing that the 
appellant had entrusted property or dominion over the 
Government property in his capacity as a public servant, or that 
he had dishonestly misappropriated or converted such property 
to his own use, the essential ingredients of criminal breach of 
trust punishable under Section 409 of the Penal Code cannot be 
said to have been established merely on the basis of suspicion.  
Considering the aforesaid facts and circumstances of the 
case, 
absence of direct evidence, contradictions and 
inconsistencies in prosecution evidence, and failure to prove 
the guilt of the convict-appellant beyond reasonable doubt by 
the prosecution and the principle of parity, the appellant is 
entitled to the acquittal.  
This Court finds that the material purchasers did not 
support the allegation of overpricing, the alleged money 

<<PAGE 19>>
 
19
receipts were not satisfactorily proved to be forged, the 
Investigating Officer did not himself seized the alleged 
receipts; and the evidence concerning the alleged amount of 
misappropriation is not free from discrepancy. These 
deficiencies go to the root of the prosecution case and create 
reasonable doubt as to the appellant’s guilt. I find sufficient 
substance in the appeal. 
Accordingly, the impugned judgment and order of 
conviction and sentence passed by the learned Special Judge, 
Rangpur suffers from illegality, impropriety and infirmity and 
cannot be sustained in law. 
In the result, the appeal is allowed. 
The judgment and order dated 29.08.2019 passed by the 
learned Special Judge; Rangpur in Special Case No. 03 of 2013 
is hereby set aside.  
The convict-appellant, Md. Shafiqul Islam is hereby 
acquitted of all charges leveled against him. 
  
The convict-appellant is released from his bail bond.

input_summary: The CONVICT-APPELLANT, a clerk-cum-typist at a government fishery hatchery, challenges the judgment and order of conviction and sentence dated 29.08.2019 passed by the Special Judge, Rangpur, under Section 409 of the Penal Code 1860 read with Section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act 1947. The prosecution case alleged that carp spawn was sold above the Government-fixed rate using money receipts said to be forged, causing loss of public revenue. The appeal is brought under Section 10(1)(a) of the Criminal Law Amendment Act 1958. The appellant argued that purchaser witnesses testified they paid only the fixed rate, that the printing witness gave adverse evidence, that the investigating officer did not seize the receipts, and that a co-accused's appellate disposal supports parity. The STATE argued that the fourteen prosecution witnesses proved the case and that the trial court's findings are sound.
explanation: The court held that the core allegation of overpricing was not established, because three purchaser witnesses consistently stated they paid the Government-fixed rate and their signatures were obtained in circumstances that cast doubt on the investigation. It found the money receipts were not satisfactorily proved to be forged, the investigating officer had not personally seized them, and the amount alleged to have been misappropriated was inconsistent. Noting that the appellant, a subordinate clerk-cum-typist, stood on an even better footing than the principal accused, who had already been acquitted on appeal, and that suspicion cannot replace proof, the court held that the essential ingredients of criminal breach of trust under Section 409 were not established beyond reasonable doubt.

This appeal, preferred under Section 10(1)(a) of the 
Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1958 is directed against the 
judgment and order dated 16.08.2023 passed by the learned 

<<PAGE 2>>
 
2
Special Judge (Senior District & Sessions Judge), Special 
Judge Court, Faridpur in Special Case No. 09 of 2022, 
corresponding to Dudak Integrated District Office, Faridpur 
Case No. 01 dated 28.01.2020, convicting the appellant under 
Section 409 of the Penal Code, 1860-read with Section 5(2) of 
the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and sentencing him to 
suffer rigorous imprisonment for a period of 05(five) years 
with a fine of Tk. 10,000/- (ten thousand), in default to suffer 
rigorous imprisonment for a period of 03(three) months. The 
appellant was, however, acquitted of the charges under section 
468, 471 and 109 of the Penal Code. 
The facts relevant for disposal of the appeal, in short, are 
that one Md. Abu Sayed, Assistant Director, the Anti-
Corruption Commission, Faridpur, lodged a First Information 
Report (FIR) stating inter alia that during an enquiry under 
Memo No. E/R 35/2018, conducted by the Anti-Corruption 
Commission, Integrated District Office, Faridpur, it was 
revealed that one Nishikanta Karmakar was the owner of 33 
decimals of land appertaining to S.A. Khatian No. 217 and Plot 
No. 347 under Surjadia Mouza, Police Station Boalmari, 

<<PAGE 3>>
 
3
District Faridpur. Subsequently, the said Nishikanta Karmakar 
left for India without leaving any heir in Bangladesh and at the 
time of B.S. record, the said property was recorded under khas 
Khatian No. 1/1 in the name of the Deputy Commissioner, 
Faridpur on behalf of the Government of Bangladesh, 
corresponding to BS Plot No. 411. 
 
On 15.04.2018, accused Minoz Saha and Gobinda Saha 
submitted an application before the Assistant Commissioner 
(Land), Boalmari seeking mutation of the land in their names 
for payment of land development tax. Despite having full 
knowledge that the land appertaining to BS Plot No. 411 and 
khas Khatian No. BS 1/1, which is government khas land was 
recorded in the name of the Deputy Commissioner, Faridpur, 
on behalf of the Government of Bangladesh, accused Md. 
Abdul Kuddus Khan concealed the said fact and submitted a 
report in favour of mutation. Accused Palash Sheikh, acting as 
Mutation Assistant, examined the papers, signed the proposal 
and placed the same before the Assistant Commissioner 
(Land). 

<<PAGE 4>>
 
4
The accused Minoz Saha and Gobinda Saha, though 
possessing no right, title or interest in the said government 
land, in collusion with each other and with dishonest intention, 
created a forged deed being Deed No. 6025 dated 20.12.1969 
of Boalmari Sub-Registry Office, falsely showing Nishikanta 
Karmakar as donor and themselves as donees/transferees in 
respect of the said 33 decimals of government land. Thereafter, 
with the assistance and cooperation of the accused Md. Abdul 
Kuddus Khan, the then acting Union Land Assistant Officer of 
Parameshwardi Union Land Office, and accused Palash 
Sheikh, Vested Property(VP)/Mutation Assistant of Upazila 
Land Office, Boalmari, the said forged deed was submitted 
before the Assistant Commissioner (Land), Boalmari Upazila 
Land Office, Faridpur, and through Mutation Case No. A.C.(L) 
IX-P-1-2316/2017-18 and U.L.O. No. IX-P-1-159/2017-18, an 
attempt was made to mutate and record the said 33 decimals of

The appellant, Abdul Kuddus Khan, was the Union Land 
Assistant Officer. His role and responsibilities were expressly 
defined above. He was responsible to independently verify the 
original ownership of the property in question; examine 
whether the deed was valid, registered, and genuine and 
confirm whether the land was subject to any government claim 
and to ascertain physical possession and payment of land 
development tax. The appellant, under the aforesaid Handbook, 
had the clear duty to verify the original ownership and 
genuineness of the deed.  
The appellant performed none of these duties. He 
submitted a false report without any independent verification. 
His act was not one of omission but of active commission with 
dishonest intention.

appellant Abdul Kuddus Khan, in collusion with the private 
accused and recommended mutation in their favour. 
The passage of 50 years without any claim, mutation, tax 
payment, or possession gives rise to suspicion of fabrication 
and forgery and proves that the mutation application was 
nothing but a fraudulent means of land grabbing. 
The trial Court, upon careful evaluation of the evidence 
and the applicable legal framework, found that Palash Sheikh 
had no statutory duty under the relevant guidelines (Handbook 
for AC Land) to verify the deed or report on the mutation 
application. His role was primarily clerical or ancillary. 
Consequently, even though he submitted a report, he could not 
be held criminally liable for failure to perform a duty that did 
not legally rest upon his office. The trial Court therefore 
acquitted him. 
The principle of parity does not apply where the roles

verifying authority under the Handbook for AC (Land), Palash

copy issuer of the alleged deed were not made accused in this 
case; as such, the conviction and sentence is not tenable in the 
eye of law. However, this Court finds no substance in the 
contention. Because non-impleadment of certain persons does 
not vitiate the FIR or the trial, so long as the core allegations 
against the appellant are made out. 
The conviction under Section 409 of the Penal Code 
(criminal breach of trust by public servant) and Section 5(2) of 
the Prevention of Corruption Act (criminal misconduct) does 
not amount to double jeopardy, as the offences are distinct in 
ingredients and the same set of facts may constitute both. 
There is no bar to conviction under both provisions.

offender and there is nothing on record to suggest that he has 
any previous criminal antecedent and the appellant is about 60 
years old.

the evidence on record, this Court is of the view that the ends

The trial court's order dated 05.07.2007 on that case and the appellate judgment dated 18.05.2017 concerning it are the orders under challenge. The Rule was issued under Section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 calling upon the OPPOSITE PARTIES to show cause why those orders should not be displaced. explanation: The court held that the final decree was drawn after the defendant's death without his heirs being substituted, so the ex parte decree and final decree could not be treated as binding on the petitioners' interests without further trial. It relied on the admission of the plaintiff's witness that the defendant had purchased land and had no objection to a retrial, treating that unrebutted position as sufficient for the ends of justice. Finding the Rule had merit, the court held the lower orders could not be sustained and restored the suit to its original file and number, with the petitioners entitled to adduce evidence in the trial.

This revisional application, at the instance of the

" Let a Rule be issued calling upon the opposite party

Concomitantly, this Court was also pleased to call for

and decree for a period of 06(six) months from date.

<<PAGE 3>>
- 3 -

Subsequently, the petitioner filed an application for an 
injunction, and after hearing, this Court was pleased to allow 
the said application with a direction upon both parties to 
maintain status quo in respect of possession and position of 
the suit property till disposal of the Rule.  
The nucleus of the facts of the instant Rule is that the 
plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 195 of 1998, subsequently 
renumbered as Title Suit No. 51 of 2015, against the 
defendants seeking partition of the ejmali property, 
declaration of title, and a declaration that the registered 
Deeds dated 04.03.1948, being Nos. 1291 and 1292, are not 
binding upon the plaintiffs. The plaintiffs' claims rested upon 
the fact that the suit property originally belonged to Rashik 
Chandra, measuring 19.69 acres, of which he sold 14.33 acres 
to Sreeram Chandra Talukdar, while the rest land remained 
with him, subject to a subsequent deduction for a 
Government Road. After Rashik Chandra's death, his alleged 
sole son, Jatindra Chandra (defendant No.14), succeeded to 
the 
remaining 
property. 
Sreeram 
Chandra thereafter 
transferred portions of the land to the plaintiffs' predecessors,

<<PAGE 4>>
- 4 -

and the plaintiffs and their predecessors subsequently 
acquired additional portions by purchase and inheritance, 
thereby becoming owners of an aggregate of 9.04 acres. The 
plaintiffs further allege that, taking advantage of an erroneous 
R.S. record-of-rights, the defendants claimed title through one 
Dhonenjoy and attempted to dispossess them, giving rise to 
the suit. 
Conversely, defendant Nos. 1–13, 15 and 35–37 
contested the suit by filing written statements. Their case, in 
substance, is that the property originally belonged to Rashik 
Chandra and was subsequently recorded in R.S. Khatian No. 
286 in the names of Rashik Chandra, Tofazzol Hossain, Moktar 
Hossain, Jalal Ahmed, Samsul Haque, Motahar Hossain, 
Nezamul Haque and Dhonenjoy in their respective shares. 
According to the defendants, Dhonenjoy owned 2.56 acres, 
which he transferred to Nurullah, Ojiullah, and Sanaullah, and 
the S.A. record was accordingly prepared in their names. The 
defendants claim possession through successive transfers and 
the present record of rights, having erected homesteads and 
planted trees on the suit land. They further contend that

<<PAGE 5>>
- 5 -

Rashik Chandra had no son named Jatindra Chandra and, 
therefore, the alleged transfer or claim founded upon Jatindra 
Chandra is fictitious and unenforceable. On these grounds, 
they prayed for dismissal of the suit. 
Thereafter, upon completion of all requisite legal 
formalities, the learned trial Court concluded the trial and, by 
its judgment and decree dated 30.11.2016, decreed the suit in 
part in respect of 8.60 acres of land. Being aggrieved and 
dissatisfied with the said judgment and decree, the contesting 
defendants preferred Title Appeal No. 13 of 2017 before the 
learned District Judge, Bhola, who subsequently transferred 
the appeal to the learned Additional District Judge, Char-
Fasson, Bhola, for hearing and disposal. 
Upon hearing the parties and perusing the materials on 
record, the learned Additional District Judge was pleased to 
allow the appeal by his judgment and decree dated 
18.10.2021, thereby reversing the judgment and decree of the 
learned trial Court. Aggrieved and dissatisfied with the said 
judgment and decree of the learned appellate Court, the

<<PAGE 6>>
- 6 -

plaintiffs have invoked the revisional jurisdiction of this 
Court.

Mrs Zubaida Gulshan Ara, learned Counsel appearing on 
behalf of the petitioners submitted that the learned trial Court 
after analyzing all the evidences on record decreeing the suit 
in preliminary form giving specific shaham to the plaintiffs, 
thus the learned appellate Court, without considering the case 
in its truest perspective and without controverting the 
reasons given by the learned trial Court allowed the appeal 
which cannot be sustain in law.   
Learned Counsel further submitted that the plaintiffs 
prayed for dispense with the liability of integration which was 
allowed by the trial Court and the defendant did not take any 
legal steps against said decisions and further question of 
defect of parties cannot arise at all, thus the learned appellate 
Court without considering the said aspect found the suit is 
barred defect of parties, and such kind of non-consideration 
of evidence and thereby committed an error of law resulting 
in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice.

<<PAGE 7>>
- 7 -

Learned Counsel further submitted that in the 'Ka' 
schedule of the plaint the entire land of C.S. Khatian No. 706 
has been mentioned as 14.33 acres and out of the aforesaid 
land 1.69 acres land has been acquired for public road by the 
government and hence the schedule 'Ka' mentioned 12.70 
acres rest land out of which the plaintiffs claimed 9.04 acres of 
land and as such there is no question in respect of hotspots is 
maintained but the learned appellate Court without 
considering the aforesaid aspect found that the suit is bed for 
hotchpots and thereby committed an error of law resulting in 
an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice.   
Learned Counsel has further posited that the possession 
of the parties is immaterial of partition suit and as such only 
considering the possession of defendants and report of 
Advocate Commissioner should not be considered as basis of 
Saham in favour of any party and hence the finding of the 
appellate Court i.e., “উেিখত কিমশন িতেবদন এবং সংি কাগজপ 
দশন-1 এবং 11 িসিরজ পযােলাচনায় দখা যায় য, নািলশী স ি!র "# দখল মূলত 
িববাদী আপীলকারী পে&র অনুকূেল মেম িতেবদন আিসয়ােছ। িক+ িব, িবচািরক 
সই কিমশন িতেবদন িবষেয় মােটও আেলাচনা কেরন নাই।", which is 
absolutely based on wrong interpretation of law and hence

<<PAGE 8>>
- 8 -

the judgment of the learned appellate Court cannot be sustain 
in law.   
Learned Counsel has further submitted that title deed of 
the defendants dated 18.3.1942 executed by Jitendra Lal and 
Shoilobala in favour of Dhonenjoy Das being deed no.244 
does not include the land of C.S. khatian no.706 
corresponding to R.S. khatian No.286 and hence the aforesaid 
transferred deed of prior owner to defendants namely 
Dhonenjoy should not be considered as the basis of claiming 
suit land and the appellate Court being misconceive about the 
said deed allowed the appeal which cannot be sustain in law.

Conversely, Mr Md. Asadur Rahman, the learned 
Counsel appearing on behalf of the opposite parties, 
submitted that the learned trial Court misconceived the facts 
and the proposition of law in decreeing the suit, whereas the 
learned appellate Court, after due analysis of the evidence on 
record, allowed the appeal, which cannot be interfered with 
by this revisional jurisdiction.

<<PAGE 9>>
- 9 -

Learned Counsel further submitted that the suit is 
seriously barred for defects of parties as one of the main 
parties, that is, the District Board, was a main party to the 
instant suit and the total land of C.S Khatian was not brought 
to the suit and as such the learned appellate Court rightly 
found that the suit of the plaintiff was not maintainable.  
Learned Counsel further submitted that subsequently 
R.S record was rightly published in the name of Dhonenjoy, 
who transferred the 2.56 acres of land to Nurullah, Ojiullah 
and Sanaullah, and S.A record has been prepared in their 
names, and the defendants are now in possession of the suit 
property by record of rights and erecting homestead as well 
as planting trees there to.  
Learned Counsel finally referred to the decisions as 
contained in 15 MLR (AD) 17 in respect of the cardinal 
principle of law that the plaintiff has to prove his case with 
cogent evidence, and he cannot rely on the weakness of the 
defendants' case. The other decisions, as reported in 51 DLR 
(AD) 155, are in respect of the hotchpotch of the partition 
suit.

<<PAGE 10>>
- 10 -

Having heard the learned Counsels appearing for the 
respective parties, perused the revisional application, the 
impugned judgment and decree, the judgments of the 
Subordinate Courts, the pleadings, the oral and documentary 
evidence available on record and the other materials annexed 
to the revisional application, this Court is called upon to 
determine whether the learned Appellate Court, in reversing 
the judgment and preliminary decree passed by the learned 
Trial Court, correctly appreciated the evidence and applied 
the governing principles of law. 
At the outset, it appears from the record that the 
original owner, namely, Rashik Chandra, was admittedly the 
owner of a total area of 14.33 acres comprised in C.S. Khatian 
No. 706. The extent of the jote, namely, 14.33 acres, is not 
seriously disputed by either side. The controversy, therefore, 
principally relates to the derivation of title to the disputed 
portion, the legal effect of the subsequent transactions, the 
evidentiary value of the respective records-of-rights, the 
parties' possession, and, further, the effect of the alleged non-
inclusion of the entire joint property in the hotchpot.

<<PAGE 11>>
- 11 -

On careful perusal of the judgment of the learned Trial 
Court, it appears that the said Court did not decree the suit 
mechanically or merely on the basis of the documentary 
record. Rather, the learned Trial Court carefully considered 
the oral testimony adduced by both sides. 
It is evident that PW-1, Shah Alam Kazi, fully supported 
the material averments made in the plaint and his testimony 
was found by the learned Trial Court to be consistent with the 
plaintiff's pleaded case. PW-2, Abul Hossain Mridha, was a 
particularly material witness. He stated that he knew both the 
plaintiffs and the defendants and that the total area of the 
land was 14.33 acres, whereas the plaintiffs' claim related to 
9.04 acres. More importantly, in cross-examination he stated 
that he was engaged in agricultural activities and cultivated 
the suit land as a bargadar. He further stated that, apart from 
the four plaintiffs, no other person was in possession of or 
cultivating the suit land. 
The significance of PW-2's testimony cannot be 
overlooked. He was not a stranger to the land or a witness

<<PAGE 12>>
- 12 -

merely speaking from hearsay. His evidence was based upon 
his 
asserted 
personal 
knowledge 
of 
cultivation 
and 
possession. The defendants had every opportunity to test his 
credibility through cross-examination. Yet, nothing material 
was elicited from his cross-examination which substantially 
undermined his testimony or established the defendants' 
asserted possession. 
Equally significant is the fact that no suggestion was put 
to PW-2 that he was inimical towards the defendants, that he 
was interested in the plaintiffs, or that he had any other 
reason to falsely depose against the defendants. Although the 
mere absence of such a suggestion is not, by itself, conclusive 
proof of credibility, such omission is nevertheless a relevant 
circumstance when the Court is assessing whether the 
witness's testimony has been effectively impeached or 
materially shaken. 
Similarly, PW-3, Shamsul Haque Majhi, stated in his 
examination-in-chief that the suit land measuring 9.04 acres 
was in the possession and enjoyment of Shah Alam and 
others. His testimony is particularly significant because it

<<PAGE 13>>
- 13 -

directly supports the plaintiffs' assertion of possession. More 
importantly, PW-3 was not cross-examined at all on behalf of 
the defendants. Consequently, the material assertions 
contained in his testimony remained wholly unchallenged. 
It is a settled principle of appreciation of evidence that 
where a witness makes a material assertion on a particular 
issue and the adverse party, having full opportunity, does not 
cross-examine the witness on that material aspect, the Court 
may legitimately take such omission into consideration in 
determining whether the assertion has remained unrebutted. 
It does not mean that an unchallenged statement 
automatically becomes conclusive proof; nevertheless, where 
such testimony is otherwise consistent with the pleadings and 
surrounding documentary evidence, the absence of cross-
examination assumes considerable evidentiary significance. 
The learned Trial Court, therefore, cannot be said to 
have acted perversely in relying upon the evidence of PW-2 
and PW-3, particularly when their evidence remained 
materially unshaken and no convincing evidence was brought 
on record to establish that the plaintiffs had been

<<PAGE 14>>
- 14 -

dispossessed or that the defendants were in actual possession 
of the disputed land. 
The principal reasoning of the learned Trial Court was 
that the defendants claimed through Dhananjay Das on the 
basis of Patta Deeds Nos. 1291 and 1292 dated 04.03.1948, 
whereas the defendants had not adequately explained the 
source of Dhananjay's title to the disputed property. 
Ordinarily, a party claiming title through a predecessor 
must establish a legally recognizable chain of title leading 
from the admitted or established owner to the claimant. A 
person cannot ordinarily convey a better title than he himself 
possesses, subject to the recognized exceptions under the 
law. Therefore, where the title of the predecessor is 
specifically challenged, it becomes incumbent upon the 
claimant to establish the root or lawful source of that 
predecessor's title. In this context, it is imperative to admit 
that a person cannot give anything beyond his interest. 
The learned Trial Court observed that Dhananjay was 
not the recorded owner in the C.S. record and that the

<<PAGE 15>>
- 15 -

defendants had not, according to the evidence then before 
that Court, satisfactorily demonstrated how Dhananjay 
acquired title from Rashik Chandra, the recorded C.S. owner. 
However, the learned Appellate Court brought on 
record and relied upon registered Deed No. 244, whereby 
Dhananjay Das was allegedly a purchaser from Jitendra Lal 
Sarkar, son of Rashik Chandra, and Shailabala Sarkar, wife of 
Rashik Chandra. According to the said deed, 3.79 acres of land 
from C.S. Khatian No. 706 were transferred in favour of 
Dhananjay. 
This document is of considerable legal significance. Once 
a registered deed tracing Dhananjay's acquisition to persons 
claiming 
through 
Rashik 
Chandra 
is 
brought 
into 
consideration, the reasoning of the learned Trial Court that 
there was absolutely no documentary basis for Dhananjay's 
subsequent claim cannot be sustained in its unqualified form 
without examining the legal effect, extent, identity and 
applicability of that deed to the suit land.

<<PAGE 16>>
- 16 -

The revisional Court must, therefore, distinguish 
between two propositions. First, the existence of Deed No. 
244 furnishes a prima facie documentary link between 
Dhananjay and persons claiming through the admitted C.S. 
owner. Secondly, the existence of that deed does not, by 
itself, conclusively establish that the entire suit land claimed 
by the defendants falls within the land validly conveyed by 
that deed. The identity and correspondence of the land 
covered by Deed No. 244 with the land presently in dispute 
must still be established by the evidence on record. 
This distinction is crucial. 
A registered instrument is not a talisman which 
automatically establishes title to every parcel mentioned or 
claimed under it. At the same time, a Court cannot disregard 
such a registered instrument merely because the transferee 
was not the original C.S. recorded tenant, particularly where 
the deed itself purports to trace the transferee's title to 
persons claiming through the original recorded owner.

<<PAGE 17>>
- 17 -

However, the record further indicates that Rashik 
Chandra had previously transferred 9.08 acres out of the total 
14.33 acres to Ram Chandra by Deed No. 2216 dated 
18.04.1941. The subsequent transaction in favour of 
Dhananjay was for 3.79 acres vide deed 244 dated 
04.03.1942. 
This 
chronological 
sequence 
assumes 
substantial 
importance. The earlier deed in favour of Ram Chandra 
necessarily requires examination before determining the 
extent of the property which remained available to Rashik 
Chandra's successors for subsequent transfer. 
Be that as it may, if Rashik Chandra had already 
conveyed 9.08 acres out of 14.33 acres, the remaining 
interest, subject to the precise identification of the land and 
the terms of the earlier conveyance, would require careful 
examination. Thereafter, the Court must determine whether 
the 3.79 acres covered by Deed No. 244 formed part of the 
remaining interest of Rashik Chandra and whether the 
vendors under that deed possessed the requisite transferable 
interest.

<<PAGE 18>>
- 18 -

The subsequent sale deeds executed by Ram Chandra, 
namely Deed Nos. 971, 972 and 973 dated 20.04.1942, are 
also relevant for determining the ultimate disposition of the 
property originally covered by the earlier transaction. Thus, 
the title dispute cannot properly be resolved by looking at 
Deed No. 244 in isolation. The entire chain of transactions has 
to be considered cumulatively. 
The fundamental principle is that title must be 
determined by examining the continuity, legality and extent 
of the chain of title, rather than by relying exclusively upon 
one isolated khatian or one isolated deed. 
However, the learned Trial Court attached considerable 
importance to C.S. Khatian No. 706, wherein Rashik Chandra 
was recorded as owner of 14.33 acres. As per the provisions of 
Section 103(5) of the Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885, such an entry, 
being an old record-of-rights, carries evidentiary value and 
gives rise to the statutory presumption attached to a properly 
prepared record-of-rights, subject to rebuttal in accordance 
with law.

<<PAGE 19>>
- 19 -

At the same time, the subsequent R.S. and S.A. records 
cannot simply be brushed aside. A subsequent record-of-
rights may constitute relevant evidence concerning possession 
and the state of the record at the time of its preparation. 
However, it is equally well settled that a record-of-rights does 
not, by itself, create title where the person in whose favour 
the entry stands has no lawful source of title. 
Thus, neither side is entitled to rely upon a khatian as 
though it were, by itself, the source of title. The correct 
approach is to examine the record of rights together with the 
deeds, succession, possession, surrounding circumstances, 
and the chain of title. If the defendants' R.S. and S.A. entries 
are supported by an antecedent lawful conveyance, those 
entries acquire greater evidentiary significance. Conversely, if 
no lawful title is established in the predecessor, the 
subsequent entries cannot independently cure the defect in 
the root of title. 
In the present case, the learned Appellate Court 
correctly noticed the existence of Deed No. 244 but, in my 
considered view, did not sufficiently undertake the further

<<PAGE 20>>
- 20 -

exercise of determining whether the 3.79 acres covered by 
that deed corresponded with the disputed land claimed by the 
defendants and whether the subsequent Patta Deeds Nos. 
1291 and 1292 were legally traceable to that acquisition. 
The defendants relied principally upon Patta Deeds Nos. 
1291 and 1292 dated 04.03.1948. The legal efficacy of those 
deeds necessarily depends upon the title and authority of the 
person who executed them. 
A transferee claiming through a deed must establish not 
merely the execution of the deed but also the transferor's 
subsisting interest in the property conveyed. The maxim nemo 
dat quod non habet embodies the basic principle that a 
person ordinarily cannot transfer a better title than he himself 
possesses. 
Therefore, the Patta Deeds could not be treated as 
conclusive proof of the defendants' title merely because they 
were executed in their favour. The Court was required to 
trace the title of Dhananjay and determine whether the land

<<PAGE 21>>
- 21 -

covered by the Patta Deeds formed part of the property 
validly acquired by him. 
The registered Deed No. 244 assumes relevance 
precisely for this reason. It supplies a potential root of title 
which was not considered by the learned Trial Court. 
However, whether that root ultimately establishes the 
defendants' title over the entire disputed 9.04 acres is a 
separate question requiring evidence and identification of the 
land. 
However, the learned Appellate Court also relied upon 
the Commission Report and observed that the Commissioner 
did not establish title and possession in favour of the 
defendants. 
In this regard, it must be remembered that an Advocate 
Commissioner appointed for local investigation ordinarily 
assists 
the 
Court 
in 
elucidating 
physical 
features, 
identification, measurement, boundaries, location, possession 
or other matters falling within the scope of the commission. A 
Commissioner is not ordinarily the adjudicator of title. The

<<PAGE 22>>
- 22 -

ultimate determination of title remains exclusively within the 
province of the Court. 
Therefore, the fact that the Commission Report did not 
itself establish title in favour of either party cannot, standing 
alone, be treated as a defect in the plaintiffs' case. Equally, the 
Report may nevertheless be highly relevant if it identifies the 
suit 
land, 
boundaries, 
road, 
physical 
features 
and 
correspondence between the land described in the deeds and 
the land found upon local investigation. 
The record indicates that the Commissioner identified 
an area of approximately 1.80 decimals relating to the road 
and that the road had been constructed during the relevant 
period of R.S. survey operation. Such factual findings may 
have significance in determining the identity and extent of the 
land, but they do not, by themselves, determine title. 
The learned Appellate Court was therefore required to 
examine the Commission Report in its proper evidentiary 
context rather than treating it as either a title deed or an 
adjudication of ownership.

<<PAGE 23>>
- 23 -

However, possession is undoubtedly an important 
evidentiary circumstance in a civil suit concerning immovable 
property. Where title is in dispute, evidence of long, 
continuous and exclusive possession may constitute a relevant 
circumstance in determining the probabilities arising from the 
competing claims. 
In the instant case, PW-2 stated that he cultivated the 
suit land as a bargadar and that, apart from the plaintiffs, no 
other persons were in possession or cultivation thereof. PW-3 
also supported the plaintiffs' possession. The defendants did 
not materially challenge these assertions. 
The learned Appellate Court, while reversing the Trial 
Court, therefore ought to have dealt specifically with these 
uncontroverted or materially unshaken pieces of evidence and 
assigned cogent reasons for rejecting them. 
An appellate Court undoubtedly has jurisdiction to 
reappraise the evidence and reach a different conclusion. But 
such jurisdiction must be exercised judicially. Where the Trial 
Court has relied upon material oral and documentary

<<PAGE 24>>
- 24 -

evidence, an appellate Court reversing such findings is 
ordinarily expected to demonstrate why the evidence relied 
upon by the Trial Court is legally or factually insufficient. 
A reversal without addressing the material reasoning of 
the Trial Court may amount to failure to exercise appellate 
jurisdiction in accordance with law. 
The appellate Court is the final Court of fact. It is 
therefore under a legal obligation to consider the evidence 
independently, address the material findings of the Trial 
Court, determine the issues arising from the pleadings and 
give reasons for accepting or rejecting the evidence. 
The appellate power to reverse a judgment is 
undoubtedly broad, but it is not arbitrary. The appellate Court 
must demonstrate a rational nexus between the evidence 
relied upon and the conclusion reached. 
In the present case, the learned Appellate Court placed 
substantial reliance upon Deed No. 244 dated 18.03.1942 [the 
record also refers to the date as 04.03.1942 in one place] but 
did not sufficiently reconcile that deed with the earlier Deed

<<PAGE 25>>
- 25 -

No. 2216 dated 18.04.1941 whereby Rashik Chandra had 
allegedly transferred 9.08 acres out of 14.33 acres to Ram 
Chandra. 
The chronological relationship between these transactions 
was fundamental to determining title. The appellate judgment 
was required to address, inter alia: 
i. what exact land was transferred by Deed No. 2216; 
ii. what land remained with Rashik Chandra thereafter; 
iii. whether the 3.79 acres covered by Deed No. 244 
formed part of such remaining land; 
iv. whether Jitendra Lal Sarkar and Shailabala Sarkar had 
the requisite title and authority to execute Deed No. 
244; 
v. whether the 3.79 acres corresponded with the 
disputed property; 
vi. whether the subsequent Patta Deeds Nos. 1291 and 
1292 related to the same land; and 
vii. whether the R.S. and S.A. entries were supported by 
the aforesaid chain of title.

<<PAGE 26>>
- 26 -

Without answering these questions, the mere existence of 
Deed No. 244 could not conclusively establish the defendants' 
title to the suit property. 
However, the proposition that an earlier registered deed is 
necessarily conclusive against a subsequent deed or record 
requires some qualification. Registration gives a registered 
instrument substantial evidentiary significance and establishes 
that the document was presented and registered in 
accordance with law. It does not, however, by itself cure want 
of title in the executant. 
The proper principle is that an earlier registered 
instrument executed by persons having transferable interest 
is ordinarily entitled to serious judicial consideration, and a 
subsequent record-of-rights or instrument cannot simply be 
preferred over it without examining the source, extent and 
continuity of title. 
Accordingly, where the vendors under an earlier registered 
deed derived their title from the admitted recorded owner, 
and the transaction is supported by the surrounding

<<PAGE 27>>
- 27 -

documentary and oral evidence, the Court should not 
disregard 
that 
transaction 
without 
cogent 
reasons. 
Conversely, the Court must still determine whether the 
vendors had title to the precise land conveyed and whether 
the land subsequently claimed corresponds with the land 
covered by the earlier deed. 
Nevertheless, the learned Counsel for the opposite parties 
relied upon the decision reported in 51 DLR (AD) 155, 
contending that the suit for partition was defective because 
the entire joint property had not been brought into the 
hotchpot. 
The principle emerging from the said decision is that, as a 
general rule, a partition suit should embrace the entire joint 
property of the parties, since piecemeal partition may give 
rise to multiplicity of litigation. However, the rule is a matter 
of general procedural convenience and is not absolute. Its 
application is subject to recognized exceptions depending on 
the nature, location, character, and circumstances of the 
property and the rights of the parties.

<<PAGE 28>>
- 28 -

The decision referred to by the learned Counsel itself 
recognizes circumstances in which relaxation may be 
permissible, including where properties are situated in 
different jurisdictions, where particular property is incapable 
of partition, where the property is impartible, where it is held 
jointly with strangers who cannot conveniently be joined, or 
where the co-sharers have agreed to partition only a portion 
while retaining the remainder in common. 
The principle of hotchpot, therefore, cannot be applied 
mechanically. The Court must ascertain whether the omission 
of a property has caused actual prejudice to the parties before 
the Court and whether the rights of any person not before the 
Court would thereby be affected. 
In the instant case, the mere assertion that the entire 
property of the jote was not brought into the hotchpot does 
not, by itself, establish that the suit was incompetent. The 
learned Appellate Court was required to demonstrate the 
actual legal prejudice caused by such omission and the 
manner in which the decree passed in the suit adversely

<<PAGE 29>>
- 29 -

affected the rights of any person who was not before the 
Court. 
Moreover, where the omitted property or the rights of 
an omitted person are not adjudicated upon, the decree in 
respect of the properties actually before the Court cannot 
ordinarily be construed as extinguishing an independent right 
of such omitted person. 
Thus, an otherwise maintainable partition suit cannot be 
defeated solely on the ground of omission unless such 
omission attracts a specific legal consequence under the 
governing law or causes prejudice of such a nature as to 
render the adjudication legally defective. 
The record further indicates that an area relating to a 
road was identified by the Commissioner and that 
governmental 
authorities, 
including 
the 
Assistant 
Commissioner (Land), Charfassion, and the Executive 
Engineer, Roads and Highways, Barishal Circle, were 
impleaded in the proceedings.

<<PAGE 30>>
- 30 -

This aspect is material. If any portion of the land has 
lawfully vested in or has been acquired by the Government or 
a public authority, such property cannot be treated as 
privately partitionable merely because it appears within a 
private schedule. At the same time, the mere existence of a 
road on or through the scheduled land does not automatically 
establish that the entire disputed property is Government 
property. 
The Court must therefore distinguish between the 
private title to the land and any public right, acquisition, 
vesting, dedication or lawful governmental interest affecting a 
particular portion thereof. 
In the present case, the Commission Report identifying 
the road area is relevant for determining the physical identity 
and extent of the land. However, the presence of a road does 
not, without more, defeat the plaintiffs' claim to the 
remaining land, nor does it establish the defendants' title to 
the private portion.

<<PAGE 31>>
- 31 -

It is true that the jurisdiction under section 115 of the 
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, is not intended to provide a 
second appeal on facts. Nevertheless, where the subordinate 
Court has committed a material error of law, misread a 
material document, omitted to consider vital evidence, or 
arrived at a conclusion which is inconsistent with the evidence 
on record, interference in revision may become warranted. 
The present case is not one where this Court is merely 
substituting its own view for a plausible view taken by the 
learned Appellate Court. Rather, the question is whether the 
learned Appellate Court, while reversing the Trial Court, 
properly considered the material evidence, particularly the 
earlier deed in favour of Ram Chandra, Deed No. 244 in favour 
of Dhananjay, the Patta Deeds, the testimony of PW-2 and 
PW-3, the C.S. Khatian and the Commission Report. 
Upon careful examination, I find that the learned 
Appellate Court gave decisive importance to Deed No. 244 
without sufficiently examining the complete chain of 
transactions and without adequately addressing the material 
evidence which weighed with the learned Trial Court.

<<PAGE 32>>
- 32 -

The appellate judgment, therefore, suffers from an 
incomplete appreciation of the evidence and a failure to 
reconcile material documentary evidence. 
Upon a cumulative assessment of the entire evidence, I 
find that the plaintiffs' case is supported by the C.S. record, 
the oral evidence concerning possession, and the chain of 
transactions, which requires consideration in light of the 
admitted original ownership of Rashik Chandra. 
PW-2's testimony regarding cultivation and possession 
remained materially unshaken. PW-3's evidence regarding 
possession was not challenged at all. The defendants failed to 
elicit any material admission from those witnesses sufficient 
to discredit their evidence. 
On the other hand, although the defendants produced 
Deed No. 244 as Exhibit-I, the legal consequence of that deed 
required a more comprehensive examination of the preceding 
and succeeding transactions. The deed may furnish a 
documentary foundation for Dhananjay's acquisition of 3.79 
acres, but the defendants' entitlement to the entire disputed

<<PAGE 33>>
- 33 -

9.04 acres could not be established merely by proving that 
one deed. 
The crucial question was not merely whether Dhananjay 
had acquired some land from persons claiming through Rashik 
Chandra; it was whether the land so acquired was the same 
land now claimed by the defendants and whether the 
subsequent Patta Deeds and records-of-rights could validly 
extend that title to the entire disputed property. 
The learned Appellate Court, in my considered view, did 
not adequately answer that question. 
The learned Trial Court, though its observation 
regarding the complete absence of any documentary basis for 
Dhananjay's title requires qualification in view of Exhibit-I, 
nevertheless correctly proceeded upon the fundamental 
principle that the defendants had to establish the lawful 
source and extent of their title. The subsequent R.S. and S.A. 
entries could not, standing alone, supply the missing root of 
title.

<<PAGE 34>>
- 34 -

Accordingly, the learned Appellate Court committed a 
material error in treating the subsequent records and the 
existence of Deed No. 244 as sufficient to displace the Trial 
Court's findings without undertaking a complete analysis of 
the entire chain of title and the identity of the land. 
Upon consideration of the pleadings, oral and 
documentary evidence, the judgments of the Subordinate 
Courts and the applicable principles of law, I am of the 
considered view that the learned Appellate Court failed to 
give due and adequate consideration to material evidence on 
record and, in particular, failed to reconcile the earlier 
transaction in favour of Ram Chandra with the subsequent 
transaction in favour of Dhananjay and the Patta Deeds relied 
upon by the defendants. 
The learned Appellate Court also failed to adequately 
consider the materially unshaken testimony of PW-2 and the 
wholly unchallenged testimony of PW-3 regarding possession. 
The evidentiary significance of the C.S. record and the 
chronological sequence of the registered transactions was 
likewise not properly addressed.

<<PAGE 35>>
- 35 -

The finding of the learned Appellate Court, therefore, 
cannot be sustained merely on the basis of Exhibit-I. The 
existence of that deed may demonstrate a possible source of 
title for Dhananjay to the extent of the land validly conveyed 
thereby, but it does not, without proper identification and 
correlation of the land, establish the defendants' title to the 
entire suit property. 
In the circumstances, I am constrained to hold that the 
learned Appellate Court, in reversing the well-reasoned 
judgment and preliminary decree of the learned Trial Court, 
misread and/or failed to properly appreciate material 
evidence and thereby arrived at findings which cannot be 
sustained in law. 
The decision reported in 51 DLR (AD) 155, relied upon 
by the learned Counsel for the opposite parties, does not 
advance the defendants' case to the extent contended. The 
said decision recognizes that the general rule requiring all 
joint properties to be brought into the hotchpot is a rule of 
convenience and that relaxation may be permissible in 
appropriate circumstances. The said principle cannot be

<<PAGE 36>>
- 36 -

converted into an inflexible rule that every omission of 
property automatically renders a partition suit incompetent, 
particularly where no prejudice to the parties before the 
Court has been demonstrated and where the rights of an 
omitted person or property are expressly left unaffected. 
At the same time, the present decree must necessarily 
be understood as operating only upon the property and rights 
properly adjudicated upon in the suit. No right of any person 
not before the Court, nor any independent right in respect of 
property not effectively adjudicated upon, can be treated as 
extinguished merely by virtue of the decree. 
For all the reasons stated above, I find that the learned 
Trial Court's judgment and preliminary decree, though 
requiring certain observations to be read in the light of 
Exhibit-I, substantially represent a proper appreciation of the 
evidence and the governing principles of law. The learned 
Appellate Court, on the other hand, committed material 
errors in reversing the same without adequately addressing 
the relevant evidence and the complete chain of title.

<<PAGE 37>>
- 37 -

Accordingly, the impugned judgment and decree of the 
learned Appellate Court are liable to be set aside. 
The plaintiffs' entitlement to saham shall, however, 
remain confined to the extent lawfully established in the 
preliminary decree, and the defendants, if otherwise entitled 
in law, shall be at liberty to seek saham in accordance with the 
applicable law and upon establishment of their lawful title, 
without thereby disturbing or diminishing the plaintiffs' and 
Government’s land in road adjudicated share. 
Considering the facts and circumstances of the case, the 
pleadings, the evidence on record and the principles of law 
discussed above, I find merit in the Rule. 
Accordingly, the Rule is made absolute. 
There shall, however, be no order as to costs. 
However, the judgment and order dated 18.10.2021, 
with the decree drawn up thereunder and signed on 
24.10.2021, passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 
Charfassion, Bhola in Title Appeal No. 13 of 2017, allowing the

<<PAGE 38>>
- 38 -

appeal and thereby reversing the judgment and decree of the 
learned Trial Court, are hereby set aside. 
Consequently, 
the 
judgment 
and 
order 
dated 
30.11.2016, with the decree drawn up thereunder and signed 
on 01.12.2016, passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd 
Court, Charfassion, Bhola in Title Suit No. 51 of 2015, 
decreeing the suit in preliminary form, are hereby restored. 
The restoration of the preliminary decree shall, 
however, be subject to the lawful rights, if any, of any person 
or authority in respect of any property not effectively 
adjudicated upon in the suit, and shall not be construed as 
adjudicating upon or extinguishing any independent right of 
an omitted person or any Government/public interest not 
falling within the scope of the present adjudication. 
The order of stay and status quo granted earlier by this 
Court is hereby recalled and vacated. 
The Office is directed to transmit the Subordinate 
Courts Records (SCR) forthwith, along with a copy of this

<<PAGE 39>>
- 39 -

judgment, 
to 
the 
concerned 
Subordinate 
Court 
for 
information and necessary action. 
Before parting with the case, this Court records its 
appreciation 
for 
the 
diligent 
assistance, 
persuasive 
submissions and valuable efforts rendered by the learned 
Counsels appearing for both sides, which have assisted the 
Court in reaching a just and lawful determination of the issues 
involved.

(  Abdur Rahman, J )
input_summary: The PETITIONERS are plaintiffs in a partition suit over jointly held land of about 14.33 acres, seeking a share and a declaration of title against DEFENDANTS who claim through deeds and later record-of-rights. The trial court decreed the suit in part in preliminary form on 30.11.2016. On the defendants' appeal, the Additional District Judge, Bhola, by judgment and decree dated 18.10.2021, reversed that decree. The petitioners invoked revisional jurisdiction under Section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 against the appellate judgment and decree, and the Rule was issued calling upon the OPPOSITE PARTIES to show cause why it should not be displaced. The petitioners argued that the appellate court ignored the trial court's reasons and unshaken witness evidence, misread the Commission report, and wrongly held the suit defective for omitting joint property. The OPPOSITE PARTIES relied on the hotchpot rule and the record-of-rights.
explanation: UNCERTAIN: the Bengal Tenancy Act 1885 is cited for the presumption attached to record-of-rights and the title analysis rests on general principles, so the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 is recorded as the governing law because the revision was brought under its Section 115. The court held that the appellate court materially erred by reversing the trial decree without examining the complete chain of title, the earlier deed, the unshaken possession evidence and the Commission report. It held that the hotchpot rule is a convenience rule that cannot defeat the suit without demonstrated prejudice. The Rule was made absolute and the trial court's preliminary decree was restored, subject to the rights of omitted persons.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BANGLADESH 
HIGH COURT DIVISION 
(SPECIAL ORIGINAL JURISDICTION) 
 
WRIT PETITION NO. 13465 of 2019 
 
IN THE MATTER OF:

      -AND-

Rafiqul Islam and another  
        
 
 
 
....Petitioners 
 
-Versus- 
The Government of the People’s Republic of Bangladesh, 
represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Primary and  
Mass Education, Bangladesh Secretariat, Ramna,  
Dhaka-1000; and others 
....Respondents 
Mr. Nur Mohammad, Advocate with 
Mr. A.K. Shamsuddin, Advocate      
....For the petitioners 
Mr. Ajit Sil, Advocate and

....For the Respondent Nos. 9-10    
 
             
Heard on 03.09.2025, 29.10.2025, 06.11.2025 and 12.11.2025  
Judgment delivered on 09.07.2026 
 
            Present: 
 
Mr. Justice Md. Shohrowardi 
               And 
Mr. Justice Dihider Masum Kabir  
 
Md. Shohrowardi, J. 
 
On an application filed under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People’s 
Republic of Bangladesh, Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show 
cause as to why the impugned judgment and order dated 05.03.2019 passed in 
Miscellaneous Appeal No.07 of 2014 by the District Judge, Bandarban (Annexure-H) 
reversing the order No.18 dated 14.05.2014 passed by Subordinate Judge, Bandarban 
in Other Class Suit No.260 of 2012 rejecting the application for temporary injunction 
should not be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal 
effect and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit 
and proper. 

<<PAGE 2>>
 
2
The relevant fact for disposal of the Rule, is that the opposite party Nos. 9 and 
10 filed Other Class Suit No. 260 of 2012 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, 
Bandarban Hill District praying for a decree of declaration that all acts done regarding 
dismissal of the petitioners from their post without showing any cause is illegal and 
not binding upon the plaintiffs and also prayed for reinstate them in service directing 
to include their name in the MPO. During pendency of the said suit, the plaintiffs filed 
an application under Order 39 Rule 1, 2 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil 
Procedure, 1908 praying for injunction restraining the defendant Nos. 1, 2 and 3 from 
appointing in the post of the petitioners and for inclusion of their names in the MPO 
and also prayed for injunction restraining the defendants from discharging their duties 
in their respective posts. After filing the said application, the defendant Nos. 1, 2 and 3 
filed written objection against the said application stating that the plaintiffs were 
suspended from the service and finally dismissed from the service after complying 
with the due process of law and the defendants were appointed in their posts in the M. 
Hossenpara Registered Primary School. After hearing both the parties, the trial Court 
by order dated 14.05.2014 rejected the application for injunction holding that no 
statement is made in the plaint that the plaintiff-petitioners were dismissed from the 
service and there is no cause of action for filing the suit and defendant Nos. 2 and 3 
were appointed in their respective post and by suppressing the fact filed the 
application for injunction and vacated the order granting ad-interim injunction against 
which, the plaintiffs filed Miscellaneous Appeal No. 07 of 2014 in the Court of 
District Judge, Bandarban who after hearing allowed the appeal holding that the 
learned Advocate for the defendants did not dispute that the petitioners are not 
Headmaster and Assistant Headmaster of the school. Therefore, no one can restrain 
the plaintiffs from discharging their duty in their respective posts, and the plaintiffs are 
entitled to get their salary and other service benefits, against which the defendant-
petitioners obtained the Rule and ad-interim order of status quo. 
Learned Advocate Mr. Nur Mohammad appearing along with the learned 
Advocate Mr. A.K. Shamsuddin on behalf of the petitioners submits that the writ 
petitioners were appointed as Headmaster and Assistant Teacher of M. Hossenpara 
Registered Non-Government Primary School and their names were included in the 
MPO and subsequently, the said school was nationalized and the service of the 
petitioners were accepted by the government as Assistant Teacher and they are now 
serving as Assistant Teacher of Maluma Government Primary School and due to 
pendency of the suit, the petitioners are not getting the promotion to the higher post 
and the appellate Court below illegally passed an order directing to pay the salary and 
service benefits to the plaintiff-respondent Nos. 9 and 10 although admittedly they 
were dismissed from service and thereby committed an error of law resulting in an 

<<PAGE 3>>
 
3
error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. He prayed for making the Rule 
absolute.   
Learned Advocate Mr. Ajit Sil, appearing on behalf of the respondent No. 1, 
submits that the plaintiff-respondent Nos. 9 and 10 were dismissed from service and 
the suit is still pending. Therefore, a direction should be given to the trial Court to 
dispose of the suit expeditiously. 
Learned Advocate Mr. Dr. Mahiuddin appearing along with the learned 
Advocate Mr. Mohammad Redwanul Karim on behalf of the respondent Nos. 9 to 10 
submits that without formal order of dismissal following the law, the petitioners were 
restrained from discharging their duty by the Managing Committee of M. Hossenpara 
Registered Non-Government Primary School and if any appointment is given in the 
vacant post, the suit filed by the petitioners will be infructuous. He further submits that 
since the plaintiffs-respondents were dismissed from service without following due 
process of law, they are entitled to service benefits and the appellate Court below, on 
consideration of the statement made by the petitioners in the application for injunction, 
legally passed the impugned judgment and order. He prayed for discharging the Rule. 
We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocate Mr. Nur 
Mohammad, who appeared along with the learned Advocate Mr. A.K. Shamsuddin on 
behalf of the petitioners, the learned Advocate Mr. Ajit Sil, who appeared on behalf of 
the respondent No. 1 and the learned Advocate Mr. Dr. Mahiuddin who appeared 
along with the learned Advocate Mr. Mohammad Redwanul Karim on behalf of the 
respondent Nos. 9 to 10, perused the writ petition, affidavit-in-opposition filed by the 
respondent Nos. 9 to 10 and the records.   
On perusal of the records, it reveals that the respondent Nos. 9 and 10 were 
appointed as Headmaster and Assistant Headmaster of M. Hossenpara Registered 
Non-Government Primary School, Lama, Bandarban and they joined in their service 
on 15.05.2006 and 19.02.2008 respectively. It has been asserted in the written 
objection that before filing the suit, the plaintiffs were dismissed from service and 
defendant Nos. 2 and 3 were appointed, and they joined in service on 27.08.2012, and 
after that, the case was filed on 10.10.2012. Nothing has been stated in the application 
for injunction filed under Order 39 Rule 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 
that the plaintiffs-respondent Nos. 9 and 10 were discharging their duty in their 
respective posts of the said school. Rather, they filed the suit for declaration that all 
acts regarding the dismissal of the plaintiffs from service are illegal and not binding 
upon the plaintiffs, which clearly proved that the plaintiff-respondent Nos. 9 and 10 
were not serving at the time of filing the said suit. Therefore, they are not entitled to 
get the service benefit at this stage.  
Admittedly, the plaintiff-respondent Nos. 9 and 10 were the Headmaster and 
Assistant Headmaster of the M. Hossenpara Registered Non-Government Primary 

<<PAGE 4>>
 
4
School and the plaintiff-respondents prayed for their reinstatement. If any appointment 
is given in the posts of Headmaster and Assistant Headmaster of M. Hossenpara 
Registered Non-Government Primary School in which the plaintiffs discharged their 
duty, the suit filed by the plaintiff-respondents will be infructuous. Therefore, the 
respondent Nos. 1 to 8 should be restrained by an order of injunction restraining them 
from appointing any other person in the posts of Headmaster and Assistant 
Headmaster of M. Hossenpara Registered Non-Government Primary School, Lama, 
Bandarban. 
In view of the above findings and observations, the Rule is disposed of.  
The respondent Nos. 1 to 8 are restrained by an order of injunction not to 
appoint anyone in the posts of Headmaster and Assistant Headmaster of M. 
Hossenpara Registered Non-Government Primary School, Lama, Bandarban till 
disposal of the Other Class Suit No. 260 of 2012 now pending in the Court of Joint 
District Judge, Bandarban Hill District.  
The trial Court is directed to dispose of the suit expeditiously, preferably 
within 6(six) months.             
 
Dihider Masum Kabir, J. 
I agree.
input_summary: The PETITIONERS are a former headmaster and assistant headmaster of a registered non-government primary school who filed a writ petition under Article 102 of the Constitution of Bangladesh against the GOVERNMENT and others, including the plaintiffs in a civil suit. The writ challenges the judgment and order dated 05.03.2019 of the District Judge, Bandarban, in a miscellaneous appeal, which reversed the Subordinate Judge's order dated 14.05.2014 on a temporary injunction application. The petitioners seek a declaration that the impugned order was passed without lawful authority. The dispute concerns the plaintiffs' claimed removal from their posts, reinstatement, and appointment of others to those posts. The petitioners argued that the appellate order wrongly directed salary to removed plaintiffs. The statutes relied on were Article 102 of the Constitution and Order 39 Rules 1 and 2 read with Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908.
explanation: UNCERTAIN: the Rule was disposed of without a clear statement on the petitioners' prayer, so REFUSED is inferred from the court giving no declaration against the appellate order and instead restraining appointments for the plaintiffs' benefit. The court held that the plaintiffs' injunction application did not state they were serving in the posts, and that the suit was filed after others had been appointed to them, so they were not entitled to service benefits at this stage. It nevertheless found that further appointments would render the suit infructuous, and therefore restrained the respondents from appointing anyone to the two posts until the suit is disposed of, with expeditious disposal directed.

Urmee Rahman, J:  
In the instant matter a Rule Nisi was issued on an application under 
Article 102 (2)(a)(i) and (ii) of the Constitution of the People’s Republic of 
Bangladesh in the following terms: 

<<PAGE 2>>
2 
 
“Let a rule Nisi be issued calling upon the respondents 
to show cause as to why the impugned order dated 
05.01.2025 (Annexure-F) passed by the respondent no. 2, the 
Additional Secretary, Ministry of Tourism and Civil aviation 
(Appellate Authority) in Appeal No. 110 dated 31.10.2024 
upholding the order dated 15.05.2024 (Annexure-E) passed 
by the respondent No. 04 refusing to issue license in favour 
of the petitioner for new travel Agency in the name of 
“Bengal Aitken Spence Travels Limited” by changing the 
name from “Mars Universal Limited” should not be declared 
to have been done without any lawful authority and is of no 
legal effect and why a direction shall not be given upon the 
respondents to issue license in favour of the petitioner for 
new Travel Agency named “Bengal Aitken Spence Travels 
Limited” by changing the name from "Mars Universal 
Limited" and/or pass such other or further, orders or order 
as to this Court may seem fit and proper.” 
Pending hearing of the Rule operation of impugned memo dated 
05.01.2025 (Annexure-F) was stayed for a period of three months, which 
has been extended from time to time. 
Relevant facts necessary for disposal of the instant Rule, in short, 
are that, the petitioner company was incorporated as ‘Mars Universal 
Limited’ under the Registrar of Joint Stock Companies and Firms (RJSC) 
and it obtained Travel Agency License, which was valid till 31st 
December, 2025. Subsequently, the company changed its name from 
‘Mars Universal Limited’ to ‘Bengal Aitken Spence Travels Limited’ and 
accordingly a certificate of incorporation pursuant to change of name was 

<<PAGE 3>>
3 
 
issued by the RJSC in its favour on 23.11.2023. After receiving the 
relevant documents in the changed name, the petitioner applied to the 
respondent No. 3 and 4 for issuance of a license as a new Travel Agency 
with all necessary papers and documents and deposited the required fee 
through treasury challan as the earlier license is not transferable as per the 
Travel Agency laws and rules.  
The Respondent No. 4 by the order dated 15.05.2024 rejected the 
petitioner’s application for issuance of license; however, without showing 
any specific reason. Being aggrieved thereby the petitioner filed an appeal 
before the respondent No. 2, the appellate authority, who by the impugned 
order dated 06.01.2025 rejected the Appeal.  
Finding no other alternative and equally efficacious remedy 
available, the petitioner has filed the instant writ petition and obtained the 
present Rule.  
  Learned Advocate Mr. Md. Yousuf Ali, with Mr. Md. Faizullah, 
appearing on behalf of the petitioner submitted that, the petitioner in 
compliance with the provisions of law applied for new travel license but 
the respondents rejected the same in an arbitrary and whimsical manner, 
which is liable to be declared to have been issued without lawful 
authority. 
Learned Advocate next submitted that, the respondent authority 
misunderstood the term ‘non-funded liabilities’, which is not actually a 
loan but is a bank guarantee and is issued as a security for the license 

<<PAGE 4>>
4 
 
against the deposit made by the Company. Therefore, there is no 
concealment of fact in the application by the petitioner. As such the 
impugned orders of refusal may be declared to be without lawful authority 
and is of no legal effect. 
He further submitted that no statutory reasons have been mentioned 
in the investigation report but the authority rejected the application in 
issuing a fresh license in favour of the petitioner only on the ground of 
defective papers, despite submitting all required documents in accordance 
with law. As such the impugned order is liable to be set aside.  
He finally submitted that the ‘Mars Universal Limited’ changed its 
name to ‘Bengal Aitken Spence Travels Limited’ following the provisions 
of Section 11(7) of the Companies Act, 1994 and obtained certificate from 
the RJSC in due process. As such the impugned orders refusing to issue 
license in the new name of the company has no lawful basis and the 
respondent authority may be directed to grant license in the name of the 
petitioner company. 
None appeared on behalf of the respondents; however, the learned 
Deputy Attorney General contested the Rule without filing any affidavit 
in opposition though he found it difficult to put forward any argument. 
His only submission is that, if the change of name of the Company is done 
in accordance with law, the impugned order rejecting the Appeal merely 
on the ground of name change cannot be said to have been done in 
accordance with law. 

<<PAGE 5>>
5 
 
Heard the learned Advocate for the respective parties, perused the 
writ petition, supplementary affidavit thereto and all the documents 
annexed therewith.  
It appears from the impugned order that, while rejecting the appeal 
the appellate authority considered a report from Bangladesh Bank 
regarding information as to any default loan in the name of the petitioner 
Company and the appellate authority also considered the reply of the 
petitioner which was sought from them. Bangladesh Bank submitted a 
report on 11. 12. 2024 stating that there is a ‘non-funded loan’ pending in 
the name of the petitioner, however, it is non-defaulted (‡Ljvcx gy³). 
Regarding the reply made by the petitioner as to name change of the 
Company it has been stated in the impugned order that, since the 
petitioner has provided untrue and deceitful information, there is no scope 
for changing the name of the company. Accordingly, the appeal was 
rejected.  
This finding of the appellate authority is beyond its jurisdiction 
inasmuch as the appropriate authority to allow the change of name of a 
registered Private Limited Company is the Registrar of Joint Stock 
Companies and Firms (RJSC) as per the Companies Act.   
Annexure-B to the writ petition is the ‘Certificate of Incorporation 
pursuant to change of name’ issued by the RJSC on 23.11.2023 by which

6

was promoted to the post of ‘Deputy Director’ on 01.10.2006 and

was allowed to go on PRL on 09.09.2021 and he retired as

06.01.2019 issued by the Ministry of Finance, Finance Division all

or delay in granting permission due to non-completion of audit 
report of any period of service of the retired employees. But the 
respondents refrained from disbursing petitioner’s pension benefits 
as yet.  
Being aggrieved thereby the petitioner served a Notice

disbursement of his lawful entitlement of pension benefits,

after completion of unblemished service the petitioner is lawfully 
entitled to get his pension benefit in due course but the respondents 
have been refrained from making the disbursement and verbally 
denying the same without any valid reason in gross violation of 
law.  
Learned Advocate next submitted that, retirement benefit is a 
property within the meaning of Article 152 of the Constitution of 
Bangladesh and the Constitution provides that no person shall be 
deprived of his property save and except by the authority of Law. 
The duty of the state to disburse the pension immediately on the 
retirement of an employee is obligatory. Withholding and denying 
the pension benefits to the petitioner is liable to be declared illegal 
and without any lawful basis.

Service Rules (BSR) Part I, Rules 242-505, there is no statutory 
basis for the sanctioning authority not to pay pension wages or 
making any delay in processing the sanction of pension if any 
period of service of the employee remains unaudited and as such 
the respondents are required to be directed to pay the pension 
benefits to the petitioner forthwith.

the petitioner that he would be paid his entitled retirement benefits 
immediately after his retirement. Despite submitting repeated

objection. But the authority is withholding the lawful entitlement of 
the petitioner in an unlawful manner.  
She also submitted that, the petitioner applied for pension in 
due process on 28.06.2022 and the department of Disaster

Ministry of Disaster Management and Relief vide memo dated 
21.08.2022. Hence, the respondents are lawfully obligated to make 
payment of the petitioner’s pension benefits at once.

objection during the service period of the petitioner, that should be 
resolved within the specified period of 3 (three) months as per the
